title: General-purpose private computation at near-plaintext cost

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to run ordinary, general-purpose programs on private data at a small measured multiple of the cost of running them openly. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) already lets a computer evaluate functions on encrypted data without decrypting it. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) already lets parties compute an agreed function of their private inputs. The advance sought here is practical efficiency across broad workloads, including long computations and data-dependent memory access.

Two related completion tracks belong to this concept. In the encrypted-outsourcing track, an evaluator processes encrypted inputs while protecting the information promised by the scheme. In the multiparty track, mutually distrusting participants jointly compute while protecting inputs against a specified set of corrupt participants. Achieving one track would not automatically establish the other: their trust assumptions, communication requirements and security guarantees differ.

As a proposed scope definition, general-purpose privacy includes protecting data-dependent memory addresses when those addresses reveal private information. Near-plaintext cost must account for the resources needed to deliver that protection, including setup, preprocessing, memory and communication under an explicit accounting or amortization rule. Arbitrary computation means support for computations of arbitrary finite length, with resources scaling accordingly; it does not mean unlimited computation at fixed cost.

significance.text: If the proposed efficiency targets were achieved, confidential cloud processing and joint statistics across independent data owners could become practical for substantially broader workloads. An outside computer could perform useful work without receiving the underlying plaintext, and organizations could obtain agreed joint results without assembling all inputs under one plaintext data custodian. The revolutionary element would be the reduced economic penalty for preserving privacy, extending capabilities that FHE and MPC already provide.

Economic interchangeability with ordinary computation is a conditional assessment. Even a low computation overhead would leave deployment dependent on setup costs, memory use, hardware, network conditions, numerical precision, permitted leakage and participant availability. The supplied survey documents substantial computational and storage overhead, difficulties combining schemes and weak multiparty scalability; it also describes techniques for deep evaluation and batching. Its evidence does not justify confining all present private computation to shallow circuits or narrow numeric workloads.

As downstream possibilities, affordable private computation could help enable private training of very large models or privacy-preserving network services. These are conditional extensions requiring additional protocol and systems work. Private evaluation alone does not settle what a released model or output reveals, or conceal all traffic patterns, timing and participation metadata.

Information-theoretic security is a separate target with its own constraints. The supplied 2021 lower-bound paper proves communication bounds in particular perfect-security models and for particular functionalities, including reactive functionalities that receive inputs over time. Its active-security result includes an Ω(n g)-bit bound for the relevant construction with n parties and g circuit gates, whose inputs scale with circuit size. The paper explicitly leaves open overhead relative to circuit size when circuits greatly exceed their inputs, and explains that this particular bound does not extend to statistical security. It therefore does not establish a blanket impossibility of communication proportional to input plus output size for computationally secure MPC.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is broad private execution with a small concrete overhead at a specified security level and under explicit resource accounting. Existing functionality and favorable asymptotic bounds do not settle this engineering goal. In particular, communication proportional to circuit size is a communication result; online runtime proportional to ordinary RAM runtime is an online result. Neither alone demonstrates low total wall-clock cost after preprocessing, networking and memory are included.

For the noise-based FHE families discussed in the April 2026 survey, maintaining deep computation requires managing accumulated ciphertext noise, with bootstrapping refreshing ciphertexts so evaluation can continue. The survey reports representative word-wise bootstrapping latencies of approximately 4–95 seconds depending on scheme and parameters, alongside millisecond-level bit-wise bootstrapping. These figures describe differing operations and configurations, not interchangeable workload benchmarks. Bit-wise schemes lack native single-instruction, multiple-data batching, but amortized and hybrid batching techniques exist; saying they simply lose all batching would obscure important progress.

Concrete FHE barriers include the cost of ciphertext arithmetic and refresh, storage overhead, parameter choices needed for security and correctness, and efficient cooperation across schemes and parties. Improvements must preserve useful computation depth and numerical behavior while reducing total resources. The survey identifies bootstrapping as a major bottleneck and reports that it can consume more than half of execution time, but that characterization is not a universal fraction for every application.

For private RAM execution and MPC, the proposed engineering challenge is to keep data-dependent access patterns private while maintaining efficient memory use and execution across long programs. Preprocessing must have a disclosed cost and reuse policy. Malicious security must also specify how many parties may be corrupt and whether an adversary can force an abort or prevent output delivery. The supplied RAM-MPC abstract establishes a relevant theoretical direction, but supplies no concrete end-to-end benchmark showing that these requirements can be met within the proposed small overhead.

current_state.text: The April 7, 2026 survey credits Gentry’s 2009 bootstrapping construction with enabling arbitrary multiplication depth, establishing that the existence of general encrypted computation is not the missing breakthrough. This historical attribution is supported here through the survey. The supplied source index also identifies Gentry’s original STOC paper, but no retained artifact of that original paper was available in the review.

The same survey characterizes FHE-operation latency as roughly 10,000 times that of unencrypted counterparts and identifies bootstrapping as a dominant overhead. This is a survey-level, operation-level characterization, not a uniform benchmark for general programs or a lower bound on achievable overhead. The review had full survey text, with the extracted mathematical text completing the latency comparison. The survey also discusses hardware acceleration and continuing efficiency limitations; the supplied evidence does not establish that accelerators benefit only small straight-line workloads.

An ePrint by Bienstock, Efron and Yeo, received October 2, 2026, describes prior honest-majority information-theoretic MPC protocols with communication as low as Õ(|C|), up to suppressed logarithmic factors, plus an additive Ω̃(n²) cost, where |C| denotes circuit size and n the party count. Its stated new contribution is to remove that quadratic barrier for specified classes of small circuits with sublinear numbers of input parties. The abstract reports security against adaptive, malicious adversaries, subject to input-party, circuit-size, depth and corruption-threshold restrictions. Thus the earlier statement that the quadratic term simply continues to dominate small circuits misses the paper’s claimed advance. These are preprint claims available here through the abstract; the full construction and exact restrictions were not inspected in the supplied review.

SUPERPACK, the 2023 ePrint by Escudero, Goyal, Polychroniadou, Song and Weng, reports online communication across all parties of 6/ε field elements per multiplication gate with circuit-dependent preprocessing, or 10/ε with circuit-independent preprocessing, for a corruption threshold t < n(1−ε). Calling these small constants requires fixing ε away from zero. They measure online, per-gate communication rather than total execution time or total preprocessing cost. The supplied review supports these figures from the retained HTML abstract, correcting the earlier attribution to inspected PDF text.

Lin, Mook and Wichs’s 2025 ePrint, “Doubly Efficient Cryptography: Commitments, Arguments and RAM MPC,” reports maliciously secure RAM-MPC in the plain model whose online runtime is proportional to the underlying RAM program’s runtime. Each party first preprocesses its input offline and can then participate in arbitrary MPC executions over that input with other parties. The construction uses doubly efficient private information retrieval and can be instantiated from Ring-LWE. The supplied evidence is a landing-page abstract; a direct PDF refetch had failed earlier. It does not provide a measured total-cost comparison demonstrating the proposed 10× target.

Taken together, these dated results establish arbitrary encrypted evaluation, improved bootstrapping techniques, strong communication bounds and theoretically efficient online RAM execution. They do not demonstrate the proposed near-plaintext targets across general workloads. The supplied record contains no bounded freshness search supporting a comprehensive assessment as of November 1, 2026. That limitation leaves the latest overall state unresolved; it does not invalidate the documented results or show that unexamined claims are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed encrypted-computation demonstration: run a specified, representative suite of general private-RAM programs of at least 10^9 primitive steps, including data-dependent accesses whose addresses remain private, at a proposed 128-bit computational security level and within 10× of plaintext wall-clock time, without a trusted enclave. Define primitive steps, word size, numerical precision and permitted leakage. The suite should exercise varied computation and memory behavior so that one favorable program cannot stand in for general-purpose performance. These numerical thresholds are proposals, not established standards or demonstrated results.
completion_criteria.label: Representative billion-step private-RAM programs run within 10× plaintext time

completion_criteria.text: Proposed multiparty demonstration: use at least three parties, specify a dishonest-majority corruption threshold, and provide malicious security with an explicit abort or output-delivery guarantee. Require total communication across parties within 10× of total input plus output size and aggregate computation within 10× of the corresponding trusted-party computation. State whether corruption is static or adaptive and identify the computational assumptions. This is a distinct, demanding proposed completion track; success on encrypted outsourcing alone would not satisfy it.
completion_criteria.label: Maliciously secure multiparty computation meets both 10× resource bounds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed resource accounting: compare matched hardware, equivalent program semantics and precision, and disclosed network bandwidth and latency. Report setup, input preprocessing, online execution, memory consumption and communication separately. The completion cost test must include these resources under a stated accounting or amortization rule, including the number of executions over which reusable work is spread. Report both elapsed time and aggregate work where relevant so that additional parties or processors do not hide the total cost.
completion_criteria.label: Full resource costs reported under matched comparisons and explicit amortization

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: release implementations, benchmark programs and inputs, security parameters, measurement procedures and enough configuration detail for independent replication. Supply security arguments covering the claimed adversary and leakage model, and correctness checks for outputs and numerical error. Independent reproduction across varied workloads would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested boundaries. No finite benchmark suite establishes literal universality, and asymptotic generality alone does not establish practical efficiency.
completion_criteria.label: Released replication materials include security arguments and correctness checks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation rule: constructions with astronomical polynomial factors fail the concrete cost test despite favorable asymptotic descriptions. Polylogarithmic slowdown qualifies only where measured overhead satisfies the same proposed 10× limit on the declared benchmark suite and under its accounting rules. Results should state the supported program sizes, memory capacities, party counts and network conditions, along with where the target ceases to hold.
completion_criteria.label: Measured overhead meets 10× within explicitly reported operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-01, “A proof that an explicit one-way function exists,” and CRY-02, “Public-key encryption from one-way functions,” concern foundational existence and construction questions. CRY-04 concerns concrete efficiency of a stronger computation service under declared assumptions. Faster private computation would not by itself prove an explicit one-way function exists or establish public-key encryption from the minimal assumption targeted by CRY-02.

Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-03, “Practically efficient post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation,” concerns hiding program implementation under a particular cryptographic security notion. CRY-04 principally concerns protecting data during computation, including access patterns within its proposed scope. Concealing a program and privately evaluating it are different guarantees; progress on either may provide useful tools without completing the other.

Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-05, “Publicly verifiable unclonable money and copy-protected programs,” targets resistance to copying or duplication. Private evaluation does not itself prevent copying ciphertexts, software or authorized outputs. CRY-06, “Practical classical verification of quantum computation,” targets confidence in the correctness of quantum work from a classical verifier. Correctness verification and input confidentiality can complement one another, but neither guarantee entails the other.

Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-07, “Position verification that works in physical spacetime,” concerns proving physical location under adversarial constraints. CRY-04 provides no physical-location guarantee. CRY-08, “Metadata-private messaging at ordinary cost,” is a closer systems neighbor: inexpensive private computation could support some components, but hiding communication relationships, timing and traffic patterns introduces separate network and protocol requirements. Neither entry subsumes the other.

Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-09, “Post-quantum timed release with a sequentiality theorem,” targets delayed access backed by a sequentiality guarantee. CRY-04 targets efficient authorized computation while preserving privacy, without supplying such a delay guarantee. CRY-10, “A conclusive quantum classification of deployed lattice encryption,” concerns the security of deployed lattice schemes against quantum attacks. Because the supplied RAM-MPC result can be instantiated from Ring-LWE, its security assumptions matter to CRY-04; that dependence does not resolve CRY-10 or establish that every private-computation approach has the same assumptions.

change_log.change: Preserved CRY-04’s identity while separating encrypted outsourcing and maliciously secure MPC into distinct completion tracks.
change_log.reason: Their shared efficiency goal does not make their trust, security and communication guarantees interchangeable.

change_log.change: Restricted noise growth and bootstrapping claims to the documented noise-based FHE families; retained parameter-dependent 4–95-second and millisecond latency figures.
change_log.reason: The evidence does not establish a universal need for bootstrapping across all private computation or a common benchmark for those different operations.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical loss-of-batching claim with the distinction between absent native bit-wise SIMD and existing amortized or hybrid batching.
change_log.reason: The full survey documents batching techniques that the earlier wording omitted.

change_log.change: Recast the approximately 10,000× latency figure as the April 2026 survey’s operation-level characterization.
change_log.reason: It is not a uniform measured slowdown for arbitrary general programs or a universal lower bound.

change_log.change: Corrected the October 2026 ePrint account to distinguish the prior additive quadratic barrier from the paper’s claimed subquadratic progress for restricted small-circuit classes.
change_log.reason: The retained abstract contradicts the earlier unqualified statement that the barrier still dominates those cases.

change_log.change: Expanded SUPERPACK’s communication figures to include both preprocessing variants, the corruption threshold and the dependence on ε.
change_log.reason: The 6/ε figure alone omitted material conditions and could misleadingly suggest an unconditional small constant.

change_log.change: Specified offline input preprocessing, malicious security, the plain model, the private-information-retrieval building block and Ring-LWE instantiation for the RAM-MPC result.
change_log.reason: These details explain the theoretical achievement while preventing proportional online runtime from being mistaken for demonstrated low total cost.

change_log.change: Corrected source-access descriptions for the MPC papers and used the survey for the Gentry historical attribution.
change_log.reason: The retained MPC evidence consists of abstracts, the RAM-MPC PDF refetch failed, and no original Gentry artifact was retained.

change_log.change: Narrowed the information-theoretic lower-bound interpretation and preserved its perfect-security, functionality and input-size qualifications.
change_log.reason: The theorem does not establish the earlier broad impossibility claim for computationally secure MPC or for circuits much larger than their inputs.

change_log.change: Retained conditional economic and downstream significance while removing categorical present-workload and accelerator restrictions.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports substantial efficiency barriers but does not establish those blanket restrictions.

change_log.change: Made the proposed demonstrations explicit about benchmark breadth, private addresses, security parameters, corruption, abort guarantees, aggregate costs and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These details make the proposal assessable and prevent hidden preprocessing, public access patterns or favorable accounting from satisfying the target.

change_log.change: Clarified that polylogarithmic overhead qualifies only if it meets the proposed measured limit, and that finite tests establish breadth rather than universality.
change_log.reason: Asymptotic descriptions and finite measurements answer different questions.

change_log.change: Added distinctions for every other supplied roster entry without merging concepts.
change_log.reason: The record needs to explain overlap while preserving separate scientific objectives.

unresolved_issues: The supplied freshness record is empty. The material does not establish a comprehensive state-of-the-art assessment or conclusively establish that all proposed targets remain unmet as of November 1, 2026.
The three MPC ePrints were represented by retained abstracts. Their full constructions, exact applicability conditions and concrete implementation performance cannot be resolved from this record.

The precise circuit classes, input-party restrictions, depth bounds and corruption thresholds of the October 2026 subquadratic result require full-paper examination; no missing numerical restrictions have been invented.
The proposed 10×, 10^9-step and 128-bit thresholds remain editorial benchmark choices. The representative workload suite, amortization rule, hardware and networking conditions have not been selected.

The feasibility of the proposed MPC communication target must be assessed for its exact functionality, security model and setup assumptions. The supplied lower-bound paper neither rules it out generally nor establishes its feasibility.
No original Gentry paper artifact was retained. The historical account relies on the full survey’s independent attribution.
The supplied material provides no end-to-end evidence resolving the cost of frontier-model training or metadata-private networking under these proposed guarantees.

brief.title: Private computing at close to ordinary cost
possible: You could ask a cloud service to run long, varied programs on encrypted data at close to ordinary computing costs. Organizations could calculate joint statistics while keeping their inputs private, without handing all their data to a shared custodian.
why: A smaller price penalty for privacy would make confidential cloud processing and collaboration between independent data owners practical for broader workloads. People could get useful results without giving the computer doing the work access to the underlying data.

sources.showed: This work constructs a way to perform general computation on encrypted data by refreshing it as computation proceeds.
sources.cited_for: It establishes that general computation on encrypted data is possible.
sources.not_established: It does not establish execution at close to ordinary computing costs.

sources.showed: Their survey identifies bootstrapping, which refreshes encrypted data so computation can continue, as a major cost. It describes improvements in speed and in processing many values together.
sources.quote:
But in practice, bootstrapping consumes over 50%
of total execution time, posing a serious obstacle to FHE adoption.
sources.cited_for: Refreshing encrypted data remains a major obstacle to affordable private computation.
sources.not_established: The reported costs do not establish a universal slowdown for whole programs or a minimum achievable cost.

sources.who: Ivan Bjerre Damgård, Boyang Li and Nikolaj Ignatieff Schwartzbach
sources.showed: They prove minimum communication requirements for particular joint computations with perfect security, meaning protection even against unlimited computing power.
sources.quote:
We prove two classes of lower bounds on the communication complexity of information-theoretically
secure multiparty computation.
sources.cited_for: Some security guarantees impose unavoidable communication costs.
sources.not_established: These bounds do not rule out the proposed communication target for schemes whose security depends on computational difficulty.

sources.who: Wei-Kai Lin, Ethan Mook and Daniel Wichs
sources.showed: They construct private joint computation that resists cheating and supports programs with memory access. After input preparation, execution time grows in proportion to the ordinary program's runtime.
sources.quote: The online run-time of each MPC execution is only proportional to the RAM run-time of the underlying program, that can be sublinear in the input size.
sources.cited_for: Private execution can have theoretically efficient runtime after input preparation.
sources.not_established: Proportional runtime does not demonstrate a small measured slowdown once preparation, memory and networking are included.

sources.who: Alexander Bienstock, Yuval Efron and Kevin Yeo
sources.showed: Their preprint reports reduced communication for restricted classes of small computations when most participants remain honest. It protects against cheating even when attackers choose whom to corrupt during execution.
sources.quote: To our knowledge, this is the first information-theoretic MPC protocol with $o(n^2)$ communication for a wide-range of circuit classes.
sources.cited_for: Communication costs can fall below a previously persistent barrier for some small computations.
sources.not_established: The result requires restrictions on computation size, depth and input holders; it does not demonstrate low total execution cost.

sources.showed: Their SUPERPACK protocol reduces communication during private joint computation even when most participants cheat. They implement it and report improved runtimes in distributed settings with moderately many participants.
sources.quote: We implement both \textsc{SuperPack} and Turbospeedz and verify with experimental results that our approach indeed leads to more competitive runtimes in distributed environments with a moderately large number of parties.
sources.cited_for: Private joint computation can achieve practical communication and runtime improvements.
sources.not_established: The communication result depends on the honest share of participants and excludes the full cost of advance preparation.

shown: General computation on encrypted data already exists. Li and collaborators describe ways to sustain long computations and reduce their costs. The remaining advance is making broad private workloads affordable.

Lin, Mook and Wichs establish private joint execution whose runtime, after preparation, scales with the ordinary program's runtime. SUPERPACK demonstrates practical improvements in distributed execution. Neither demonstrates the proposed total-cost target across general workloads.
missing: Broad, long-running encrypted programs have yet to demonstrate the proposed small slowdown while hiding memory access patterns.
Private joint computation has yet to demonstrate both proposed resource bounds while protecting against a dishonest majority.
A complete cost demonstration must include preparation, memory and networking, with explicit rules for spreading reusable costs across executions.

milestones.label: Billion-step programs run privately near ordinary speed
milestones.explanation: Varied programs would have to meet the proposed time and security targets while hiding memory addresses, without a trusted hardware enclave. This would test affordable encrypted execution over long runs.

milestones.label: Private joint computation meets both resource limits
milestones.explanation: Participants would have to meet both proposed 10× resource bounds despite a dishonest majority, with explicit guarantees about stopping or delivering results. This would establish the separate joint-computation track.

milestones.label: Matched comparisons account for every resource cost
milestones.explanation: Comparisons would have to match hardware, program behavior and precision, and disclose network conditions and all resource costs under explicit reuse rules. This would prevent preparation or extra processors from hiding costs.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce secure and correct execution
milestones.explanation: Released software, benchmarks, security arguments and correctness checks would have to support independent reproduction across varied workloads. This would establish breadth within the tested boundaries.

milestones.label: Measured overhead stays within the declared operating limits
milestones.explanation: Measured overhead would have to remain within 10× under the accounting rules, with supported program sizes, memory, participant counts and networks stated. This would distinguish practical efficiency from favorable growth rates.

uncertain: The proposed performance and security thresholds are benchmark choices; representative workloads and cost-sharing rules remain unsettled.
Whether the joint-computation communication target is achievable depends on the exact task, security guarantees and setup assumptions.
Cheap private execution alone does not determine what released results reveal or hide timing, traffic and participation.

page.title: Fully homomorphic encryption within 10× plaintext runtime
page.definition: A programmable accelerator runs fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), which evaluates arbitrary circuits on encrypted data without the decryption key, within DARPA’s application runtime targets relative to unencrypted computation.

goal.need: Li and colleagues’ survey, published on 7 April 2026, reports FHE operation latencies about 10,000× their unencrypted counterparts and representative word-wise bootstrapping times of 4–95 s. Bootstrapping refreshes ciphertext noise so computation can continue. Reducing this overhead addresses the cost of outsourcing computation without disclosing plaintext to its evaluator. These figures concern operations, rather than general-program benchmarks.

statements.body: DARPA, Data Protection in Virtual Environments programme
statements.quote: Execution of government defined FHE applications in time scales 10x or less of unencrypted computation
statements.context: One of the technical challenges published in the programme’s special notice dated 12 February 2020.

statements.quote: To be useful, FHE must significantly close the computation gap (within 10x) to make encrypted processing practical.

completion.title: An FHE accelerator meets DPRIVE’s final logistic-regression and CNN runtime targets.
completion.criterion: A fabricated, CPU-connected FHE accelerator executes DARPA’s specified seven-layer convolutional neural network on CIFAR-10: inference ≤25 ms per image and training for 10 epochs ≤10 h, each labelled 10× plaintext runtime. It also executes 1,024-point logistic regression in ≤0.1 ms. The specified CNN uses ReLU activations. The accelerator supports BGV and parameter ranges of plaintext modulus 2–1,024, ciphertext modulus 2^15–2^500 and ring dimension 512–16,384.
completion.set_by: DARPA, DPRIVE announcement HR001120S0032, amended 19 March 2020, Phase 3; units and training duration appear in its programme-metrics chart.
completion.basis: DPRIVE supplies numerical application tests for encrypted outsourcing. These benchmarks do not establish arbitrary-program efficiency, private memory access or total MPC cost. A 2026 paper reports 22.4 ms CNN inference on an RTX 5090 after replacing ReLU activations with quadratic functions; that result does not establish the specified accelerator or encrypted training test.

milestones.title: A working FHE implementation evaluates circuits and refreshes ciphertexts without the decryption key.
milestones.criterion: Implement correct circuit evaluation with decryption complexity bounded by the security parameter independently of circuit size, including bootstrapping to refresh ciphertexts. Gentry and Halevi’s 2011 implementation tested lattice dimensions 512, 2,048, 8,192 and 32,768. One bootstrap took 30 s at dimension 2,048 and 30 min at dimension 32,768 on a single-CPU 64-bit machine.
milestones.set_by: Cryptography community convention: compact evaluation of all circuits, formalised in Gentry’s Definition 2.1.4 and implemented by Gentry and Halevi.

milestones.title: An FHE accelerator emulator executes 1,024-point logistic regression in less than 10 ms.
milestones.criterion: Execute the government-defined encrypted logistic-regression problem on 1,024 data points in <10 ms using a circuit emulator. TREBUCHET’s 2023 paper reports single-tile kernel emulation and modeled logistic-regression training times; it does not establish this complete application test.

milestones.title: A full FHE accelerator emulator performs seven-layer CNN inference in less than 250 ms per image.
milestones.criterion: Execute the government-specified seven-layer CNN on encrypted CIFAR-10 images using full-accelerator emulation in <250 ms per image. DARPA describes this as within 100× plaintext execution on a standard workstation.

milestones.title: Hardware performs the specified encrypted seven-layer CNN inference in ≤25 ms per image.
milestones.criterion: Execute DARPA’s specified seven-layer CNN, including its ReLU activations, on encrypted CIFAR-10 images in ≤25 ms per image. Choi and colleagues’ peer-reviewed 2026 paper reports 22.4 ms CNN inference on one NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU using quadratic replacements for ReLU. That demonstrates the latency with a modified network, leaving conformity to the specified network unresolved.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, DPRIVE announcement HR001120S0032, inference component of the Phase 3 application test.

not_found: Searches for DARPA programme, homomorphic-encryption standard and MPC roadmap targets found no common completion test covering general-purpose private RAM execution and malicious MPC at near-plaintext total cost.
No public result establishing all DPRIVE final application metrics on a fabricated accelerator was found.
No complete DPRIVE accounting rule covering setup, preprocessing, memory, communication and private memory access was found.

results.finding: Gentry and Halevi’s FHE implementation tested four lattice dimensions; one bootstrap took 30 seconds at dimension 2,048.
results.detail: The authors report implementing all aspects of the fully homomorphic scheme, including bootstrapping. The timing was measured on a single-CPU, 64-bit machine with large memory.
results.quote: The time to run one bootstrapping operation (on a 1-CPU 64-bit machine with large memory) ranges from 30 seconds for the "small" setting to 30 minutes for the "large" setting.

results.finding: TFHE reports a 13 ms single-core bootstrap; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The paper describes bootstrapped binary gates and circuit bootstrapping, but the supplied text does not establish the required bound on decryption complexity independently of circuit size.
results.quote: As a consequence of this result and of other optimizations, we decrease the running time of their bootstrapping from 690ms to 13ms single core, using 16MB bootstrapping key instead of 1GB, and preserving the security parameter.

results.finding: TREBUCHET SerDes CNN inference estimate: about 200 ms; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The result is a modeled performance estimate, not a full-accelerator emulation result. The text does not specify the CNN’s layer count or identify the images as CIFAR-10.
